findings.source_passage: no one now takes a nap, as they call it, without drawing his feet out of the stirrups, and leaning upon his lance, as the knights-errant used to do
findings.source_locator: Don Quixote's long speech on the depraved age, middle of the chivalry lament paragraph
findings.why_it_matters: This specific, vivid image of the knight napping in the saddle is a characteristic piece of Cervantine comic-heroic detail that anchors the lament in physical reality; its absence flattens the rhetorical texture of the speech.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the sentence about taking a nap without drawing feet from the stirrups and leaning on the lance between the armour-rustling observation and the beach/bark passage.

findings.source_passage: I am not versed in stories, said Don Quixote; but I know the oath is a good one, because I know the barber to be an honest fellow
findings.source_locator: After the barber's oath by the ballad of the curate, before the curate goes bail
findings.why_it_matters: This small exchange is a characteristic piece of Cervantine ironic character-drawing—Don Quixote's trusting naivety and dry wit are on display; collapsing it erases a moment of voice that also signals his residual sanity.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the three-line exchange: barber's oath by the ballad, Don Quixote's 'I am not versed in stories but I know the oath is a good one,' and the curate's going bail.

findings.source_passage: he said the governor was against him, not to lose the presents his relations made him for reporting him still mad but with lucid intervals; and that the worst foe he had in his misfortune was his large property
findings.source_locator: Barber's tale, during the chaplain's interview with the licentiate
findings.why_it_matters: This passage is interpretively important: the licentiate's accusation about property and corrupt governors mirrors Don Quixote's own situation and is the satirical core of the embedded tale; its omission removes the allegorical bite.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the licentiate's speech about the governor taking presents and the worst enemy being his large property, which his relations want to enjoy—this is the thematic heart of the anecdote.

findings.source_passage: yielding to the enjoyment of hearing such nonsense, he asked him what was his notion of the features of Reinaldos of Montalban
findings.source_locator: Narrator's aside before the portraits of the Twelve Peers
findings.why_it_matters: The narratorial aside 'yielding to the enjoyment of hearing such nonsense' is a characteristic ironic intrusion that keeps the reader aware of the comedy; its loss is a minor but real instance of voice flattening.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the parenthetical 'yielding to the enjoyment of hearing such nonsense' before the curate's question about Reinaldos.

summary: Three medium-severity findings—loss of the saddle-nap image in Don Quixote's chivalry lament, erasure of the barber's oath exchange and Don Quixote's dry reply, and omission of the licentiate's satirically loaded speech about property and corrupt governors—cumulatively trigger regeneration.
